meta_title: Choco Alternative for Food Distributors in 2026
meta_desc: Keep Choco and add voice ordering beside it. Your accounts speak each order into an app and approve every line. A Choco alternative that replaces nothing.

hero.h1: Looking For A Choco Alternative For Voice Ordering?
hero.lead: Add voice ordering without giving anything up. VoiceOrder Solutions runs alongside Choco: kitchens talk through what they are short of in our app, confirm each item, then send. It lands on your desk numbered and dated, by email or straight into your system, while Choco keeps its storefront and customer tools.

problem.h2: Why teams look for an alternative to Choco
problem.lead: Choco calls itself an AI platform for food and beverage wholesalers. It digitizes inbound orders, runs an online catalog that recommends items, and carries a sales hub and a foodservice CRM. None of that is a flaw. The gap that starts a Choco alternative search is usually one step wide, and replacing a whole platform to close it is out of proportion.

cards.h3: Some kitchens never take to tapping through an app
cards.body: Every ordering platform has some accounts that keep calling, texting or leaving a voicemail at 10pm. They like the person on the other end more than a screen of buttons, and those are the orders that still eat your morning.

cards.h3: A parsed message still gets read by you
cards.body: Choco's OrderAgent lifts an order out of a voicemail, a text, even a snapshot of a handwritten pad, which is a genuinely clever bit of engineering. But the cook who left that note never saw the lines your desk ended up with.

cards.h3: You want one step fixed, not a new stack
cards.body: Swapping Choco out would mean rebuilding the storefront, the sales routine and the customer records your reps lean on. That is a lot of change to buy when the trouble is the telephone.

features.h2: The Choco alternative that leaves Choco in place

rows.h3: Built by whoever is standing in the cooler
rows.body: Your account opens the app, presses to speak, and says what the kitchen is short of. Every item appears as a line with a quantity against it. They review it, change what needs changing, and only then does it leave.
bullets: Nothing is sent until your customer has looked at the list
Works from the cooler or the prep bench, at any hour
Their own phone, iOS or Android, nothing issued
20 to 30 minutes back against the same order by phone
Reps stop writing up reorders from accounts on the app, so that time goes into selling

rows.h3: One item list per account, built from yours
rows.body: Pass us the guides you keep per customer. We load them against your SKUs at the price you hold for that account, so a spoken item lands on the right row against your own SKU.
bullets: A kitchen only ever sees what it actually buys
The catalog and the pricing stay yours to set
Edit a list once and it holds on the orders after
No browsing and no cart to abandon

rows.h3: It arrives however your office likes it
rows.body: Nobody has to move desks for this. A finished order goes out as an email with a PDF, Excel or Word file attached, or straight into your ERP over the API, over EDI, or into QuickBooks.
bullets: Addressed to a rep, or to the purchasing desk
On a direct feed there is no rekeying at your end
Picking, billing and delivery carry on unchanged
No part of your stack has to be retired first

rows.h3: Stock you can see while the orders arrive
rows.body: VoiceOrder Solutions shows real-time inventory visibility tied to what is being ordered, and the catalog updates as stock levels change. It is not the system of record for stock: yours stays in charge, and a demo shows how the levels connect.
bullets: Every line you carry, not only the quick movers
Fewer stockout surprises on a late, heavy order
Numbers come out of whatever you count with now

cards.h2: How Choco and VoiceOrder Solutions split the work
cards.lead: We are not a Choco replacement, and we would rather you did not treat us as one. Our app adds on, so a storefront that is already in place has nothing to undo before you try it.

items.h3: Let the catalog sell, and let voice take the order
items.body: A storefront that suggests items earns its keep on a buyer who is browsing with time to spare. The reorder at the end of a shift is not that moment. The two jobs can sit together without arguing.

items.h3: Give each account the way in it prefers
items.body: Kitchens that are happy tapping through Choco's app can stay there. Offer the voice app to the ones who still call or text, which is where speaking the order helps most.

items.h3: Orders land where they already land
items.body: Whatever you add, the order still arrives into the system you chose, by EDI, API or QuickBooks, or by email to your desk. Nobody has to learn a new screen to receive it.

midcta.h3: See where voice ordering fits beside Choco
midcta.body: Twenty minutes. One spoken order, end to end, and the time it gives back on the next one.

steps.h2: Short enough to finish this week
steps.lead: There is no data project at the front of this, and nothing inside Choco changes. You send item lists, we set the customers up, and your customers begin sending orders.

items.body: A spreadsheet is fine. Each account's items and your prices go into a single admin screen, lined up with your SKUs.
We set up each account, and the customer downloads the app. Most have sent something in by the end of the day.
Approved by the customer, carrying a number and a time, in the shape your system expects.

faq.h2: Better than Choco, or better beside it?

items.q: Do I need a Choco alternative to get voice ordering?
items.a: No. You can keep Choco exactly as it is and add VoiceOrder Solutions next to it. Accounts keen to talk get our app; the ones happy in Choco's app stay put. Nothing has to be switched off first, and nothing in Choco has to change.

items.q: Would that make VoiceOrder Solutions a Choco competitor?
items.a: Only in the narrow sense that both take orders. We do not run storefronts, sales tooling or a CRM, and we do not want you to give those up. Most people who search for a Choco alternative want one thing added, an order the kitchen speaks and approves, rather than a platform taken away.

items.q: Is VoiceOrder Solutions better than Choco?
items.a: Not at what Choco is built for: bigger baskets, rep tooling and customer records. Where we are stronger is narrower. The customer approves every item before it goes, so nobody at your end interprets a message. That is why we belong beside Choco, not in its place.

items.q: Does VoiceOrder Solutions connect to Choco?
items.a: No. The two are separate products, and each vendor supports only its own. Each one sends its orders into your system on its own, ours in the formats shown above, so they reach your desk in a form it already handles.

items.q: Won't some kitchens end up with two ordering apps?
items.a: Only if you set it up that way, and mostly you should not. Leave the accounts that like Choco's app where they are and offer ours to the ones still on the phone. Calls keep coming to your desk as they do today, just without an order number from us, because only what is sent through our app gets one.

items.q: How soon can our accounts start?
items.a: Most distributors are up and running within 24 to 48 hours, and most of their customers place a first order that same day. There is no IT project, and Choco carries on as normal throughout, so there is no cut-over date to plan around.

items.q: What does adding VoiceOrder Solutions cost?
items.a: We quote each distributor separately and list no prices. Choco's own pricing page says it charges a monthly fee based on usage and asks you to talk to sales. Since you would be keeping Choco, the useful question is what the voice step adds on top, and a quote answers it.

items.q: Where do the Choco details on this page come from?
items.a: Choco's own site, read on 10 October 2026: the module names and descriptions off the homepage and the usage-based line off their pricing page. We have not repeated the growth figures they publish, because those are their numbers and not ours to vouch for. If any of it has moved on since, this page is what needs correcting.
